results.corrected_extracted: Nine register studies (Finland, Sweden, Germany, the UK, European pharmacovigilance) all pointed to rising deaths involving gabapentinoids, mainly pregabalin, nearly always with other drugs, mostly opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol and antidepressants. US poison-centre annual reports: fatality records involving a gabapentinoid 38 of 2,576 (1.5%) in 2012, 41 of 2,113 (1.9%) in 2013, 41 of 1,408 (2.9%) in 2014 and 59 of 1,371 (4.3%) in 2015; pregabalin-related deaths always with other medicines; in each of 2013-2015 one record (0.05-0.07% of all fatality records), always gabapentin, attributed to a gabapentinoid alone, with no information on blood levels or autopsy. The authors sum up that pure overdoses appeared relatively safe but can become lethal in mixtures, mostly with opioids and sedatives.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors suggest that fentanyl, which accumulates in fat with repeated use and can take weeks to clear, can be displaced by buprenorphine, and that this may contribute to withdrawal within 48 hours of fentanyl use even with conventional starting procedures; they hypothesize that severe withdrawal after methadone may reflect poorly managed withdrawal from too little opioid effect early in treatment, because first outpatient doses are capped and methadone takes more than a week to reach steady levels. The Conclusions say that people who take buprenorphine within 24 to 48 hours of fentanyl are at significantly greater risk of severe withdrawal than those who wait more than 48 hours, a comparison the model did not make (the paper names no reference group; by the editors' reconstruction it was the 1 week-1 month group).
results.note: Discussion paragraph 2 hedges both explanations ('may contribute'; 'We hypothesize ... may have'); the reference group is the editors' reconstruction, not stated in the paper. Hedges and attribution restored.

results.corrected_extracted: Scoping review by authors from a university department of biomedical sciences and public health in Ancona and an institute of emerging health professions in Philadelphia, partly funded by the Italian government's Department of Antidrug Policy: 31 designer benzodiazepines considered; PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar and Web of Science searched to March 2021, with agency reports; references reviewed for relevance by one author; included were reports in which a designer benzodiazepine was the sole or explicit contributory cause of poisoning, driving impairment or death; of 372 potentially relevant reports, 324 were excluded and 49 included, on 12 drugs; 254 cases reported 2008-2021: 1 drug offence, 2 self-administration studies, 3 outpatient admissions, 44 emergency-department admissions, 63 DUID and 141 deaths, tabulated in Table 1. Most patients and decedents were young, of both sexes, often with a history of substance use and mental illness; cases came from Finland, Germany, Japan, Norway, Poland, Sweden, the UK and the USA. The included reports are not appraised.

results.corrected_extracted: Few pharmacokinetic studies exist, so concentrations are currently hard to relate to effects; diclazepam, etizolam and phenazepam blood concentrations overlapped in impaired and non-impaired drivers, and etizolam and flualprazolam concentrations were similar in DUID cases and deaths (the authors suggest differences in tolerance); because polypharmacy is the rule, causation often cannot be assigned to a single drug; many people exposed may never develop significant adverse events (citing Carpenter et al.); many cases go undetected for lack of analytical methods or awareness; the newest drugs may cross-react with common benzodiazepine immunoassays, which often cannot tell designer from prescribed benzodiazepines; how pathologists and toxicologists attribute the role of these drugs in deaths is largely unknown.

key_findings.correction: Case reports (36 gabapentin and 19 pregabalin case presentations): the text calls tolerance and withdrawal common (27/36, 75%, and 16/19, 84%; by Table 2 these are the counts with withdrawal symptoms, and tolerance or withdrawal is recorded for 28/36 and 19/19, editors' count); behavioural dependence was far rarer with gabapentin (3/36, 8%) than pregabalin (15/19, 79%); three or more criteria in 5/36 (14%) and 13/19 (68%); transition from prescribed doses to self-administration in 10/36 (28%) and 16/19 (84%); self-administration for more than a year in no gabapentin and 3 pregabalin reports (2 to 4 years); relapse in 1 gabapentin and 2 pregabalin reports; only three cases met more than four of the six criteria (two pregabalin, one gabapentin).

Withdrawal: 25 of the 36 gabapentin case presentations concerned only withdrawal symptoms or rebound of psychiatric symptoms after stopping therapeutic gabapentin; the withdrawal described resembled benzodiazepine withdrawal (including seizures and delirium) or SSRI withdrawal, and appeared to respond poorly to benzodiazepines but improved after a gabapentinoid was reinstated and tapered.

Non-fatal overdoses: 9 gabapentin case presentations and one case series (20 pure gabapentin exposures reported to three poison centres, 9 with symptoms, none admitted); the highest gabapentin blood levels, 104.5 and 126.8 mg/L, came with coma, respiratory depression or cardiopulmonary resuscitation, both with other medicines taken; one case attributed to a pure pregabalin overdose (the man denied taking other drugs) showed coma and respiratory depression and received mechanical ventilation; a US poison-centre analysis of 94 gabapentin and 18 pregabalin overdoses found no severe outcome and no death.

Seizures: of 10 young adults seen at a Belfast emergency department after recreational pregabalin use (Millar et al., 2013), 6 (60%) had seizures, 5 of them first seizures, and 2 (20%) needed intubation, ventilation and intensive care; Table 3 notes that the contribution of other drugs, addiction history and comorbidity are not known.

Why people with other substance use prefer pregabalin, as the authors explain it ('most likely'): faster absorption (peak blood level within 1.5 hours), higher oral bioavailability (above 90% against 33-66% for gabapentin), absorption proportional to dose (gabapentin's is saturable), and a stronger inhibitory action on the alpha2-delta subunits of the calcium channels, giving a faster and stronger high.

key_findings.correction: The authors suggest that fentanyl accumulates in fat with repeated use and can take weeks to clear through the kidneys (citing their own study), and that buprenorphine displacing it may contribute to precipitated withdrawal within 48 hours of fentanyl use even when clinicians follow conventional induction procedures; they hypothesize that severe withdrawal after methadone may reflect poorly managed withdrawal from too little opioid effect early in treatment, since first outpatient doses are capped and methadone takes more than a week to reach steady levels.

key_findings.correction: Mistaken identities in the cases: seven young people were taken to emergency departments after taking a benzodiazepine they thought was alprazolam (three sedated with verbal impairment, two with CNS depression, two without symptoms; flualprazolam not confirmed in three); flubromazolam was identified in Sweden in 10 seized white tablets labelled 'XANAX' and reported to the EMCDDA in October 2014; three children were found drowsy and unsteady after eating coloured pills thought to be sweets (etizolam confirmed in one); a fatal case reported under the title 'The adulterated XANAX pill' involved etizolam with caffeine.

Concentrations do not separate harm from no harm: diclazepam, etizolam and phenazepam blood concentrations overlapped between impaired and unimpaired drivers, and etizolam and flualprazolam concentrations were similar in DUID cases and deaths; the authors suggest differences in tolerance after frequent use, and say concentrations are currently hard to relate to effects because few pharmacokinetic studies were performed.
